lessonRef.title: Concept model B: comparative thesis construction

studentTask.text: Today's focus: comparative thesis construction. Essential question: How does close, evidence-governed attention to comparative thesis construction change what a reader or writer is entitled to claim? By the end of this lesson you should be able to: Explain what comparative thesis construction means and name the textual signal that tells you it is in play. You'll need: course notebook or digital equivalent; the unit's assigned texts, in an accessible reading representation; citation reference or style manual appropriate to the course.

guidedSupport.text:
Work through this with a facilitator, tutor, or on your own if you're ready:
- Welcome and retrieval: Open with a short retrieval prompt on today's lesson. Ask the learner to predict, recall, or pose a question before any instruction.
- Model or mini-lesson: Name the move, show a worked example on a short passage, and make the success criteria explicit before practice begins. Keep the explanation centered on today's lesson.
- Guided practice: Work two supported examples together. After each step ask, "What in the text licenses that move?" Fade prompts on the second example. The object of practice is today's lesson.

If you get stuck:
- If prerequisite gap: Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for today's lesson, re-teach it on a short passage, then retry one fresh item. Do not write the learner's response.
- If repeated error pattern: Describe the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a correct case, and schedule a short later review of today's lesson.
- If procedure without understanding: Ask the learner to explain why the move for today's lesson works on this text before continuing. Accept explanation in any modality.
